subject: Copywriting
title: The Headline: Your One Shot
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Headline: Your One Shot.

hook.text: Ogilvy said: 'Five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy.' The headline IS the ad for most.

buildup.text: In a sales letter, the headline appears after the salutation. It's often bold, sometimes in a different color or font.

discovery.text: Winning headline formulas: 'How to...' 'The Secret of...' 'Warning:...' 'At Last...' Each triggers a different emotion.

twist.text: The headline doesn't need to be clever. 'How to Win Friends and Influence People' is plain—but specific and beneficial.

climax.text: Test headlines before anything else. A headline change can multiply response 19x. No other element has that leverage.

punchline.text: 19x from one headline change. No other element has that leverage.

quiz.question: According to Ogilvy, how many more people read the headline than the body?

details.summary: The headline determines whether 80% of readers continue or leave. Legendary copywriter David Ogilvy said he spent more time on headlines than on the body copy. A great headline makes a specific promise, creates curiosity, and speaks directly to the reader's self-interest.
details.whyItMatters: Headlines are the most important words in any piece of copy. Whether it's a sales letter, blog post, or landing page, the headline decides whether the rest of your work gets read or ignored.
takeaways: 80% of readers never get past the headline
Headlines with specific numbers outperform vague promises
The best headlines combine a benefit with a curiosity gap

faq.question: What makes a headline effective?
faq.answer: Effective headlines make a specific, believable promise that speaks to the reader's self-interest. 'How to Win Friends and Influence People' works because it promises a specific, desirable outcome. Add urgency, curiosity, or a fresh angle to increase stopping power.

faq.question: How many headlines should you write before choosing one?
faq.answer: Top copywriters write 50 to 100 headline variations before choosing the winner. Eugene Schwartz wrote hundreds. A/B testing then validates the choice with real data. The headline is too important to settle for the first idea.
